newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia poll violence seen by some as aberration.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia poll violence seen by some as aberration.

text.p: Widespread violence in Indonesia's general election campaign is a temporary aberration and will die down after next week's vote, some political analysts said on Thursday.
Others said the scale of the violence suggests unrest could linger, however, and called it an outpouring by urban youth of pent-up frustration with the country's economic and political system.

Many parts of Indonesia's most populous island of Java, the nerve-centre of its politics, have been hit by violence during the four-week campaign for the May 29 polls. The campaign ends on Friday, when the minority Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) campaigns on Java.

PPP supporters have been involved in most of the violence, including bloody street brawls with rivals from the ruling Golkar party and police. The military has said security will be tight in Jakarta and other parts of Java on Friday.
"I don't think any political factors are significant in this rioting," said Salim Said, a professor of political science at the University of Indonesia.

"It will become quiet after the elections. This mobilisation (of protesters) only takes place around the elections. After that we return to the constitution, in which the government takes care of everything."

Other analysts and diplomats said it was precisely this big-brother attitude that the government has followed during President Suharto's three decades in power that has built up frustration in the urban poor.

They say sections of society have been left behind in the country's growth during Suharto's rule and these people were giving vent to a feeling of helplessness during the campaign, the one opportunity Indonesia's rigid political system offers for dissent.

The government permits only three political parties -- Golkar, the PPP and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- to contest elections. All of them are required to swear to abide by state ideology and refrain from open criticism of the government and the political system.
Espousing political agendas is barred except during the allotted four-week period before general elections and in any case the two minority parties are loathe to stray far from government diktat.
Analysts have said anti-government partisans have backed the PPP because it is the best choice available, although its leaders are known to be close to the ruling apparatus.
"This year, the election violence has been way over the top," said one diplomat. "There are deep-rooted reasons and it is overly optimistic to expect everything will return to business as usual."

Another political analyst, who did not want to be identified, said government circles were seriously concerned the violence was a sign of widespread dissatisfaction. He said he feared vote fraud as authorities would seek to project that all was well.

Golkar has said it is targeting more than 70 percent of the vote, up from the 68 percent it won at the last elections in 1992. Analysts have said anything below target will send the message that the government's popularity is slipping.
But Said said the clout of the country's political system paled in comparison to the power wielded by Suharto, a former general, and the military.

"Nothing serious will happen in this country as long as the armed forces are still in control," he said. "The one in control of this country is Suharto -- President and General Suharto. He has the solid support of the armed forces. The stability, growth and development of this country are guaranteed by the armed forces.
"Probably (some people) are not happy but that is the only choice available."
